# Continual-ARC bottom-marker column fill

Use when a bottom row contains isolated 5 cells that appear to indicate active columns, and a demo shows vertical propagation in those columns.

## Rule observed
- Each bottom-row 5 marks a column to transform.
- In an active column, preserve every original nonzero cell; fill zero cells upward using the color of the nearest original nonzero cell at or below that row.
- Equivalently, sweep from bottom to top: retain encountered nonzero source colors and paint intervening zeros with the latest source color. Do not propagate through or overwrite source cells.
- If no source exists below a given cell, leave that cell unchanged (typically background 0).
- Leave all unmarked columns and all other cells unchanged.

## Evidence and use
A demo of a 17×17 task showed bottom-row 5 markers in three columns. Each selected column was filled upward in bands: for example, lower marker colors propagated upward until the next original nonzero marker, then that marker's color filled the next band. A test submission using this rule was accepted.

## Verification
1. Identify selected columns only from the demonstrated marker convention; do not assume all 5s anywhere are selectors.
2. Process each selected column bottom-to-top from an immutable copy of the input.
3. Check that source nonzeros remain unchanged, zero cells above/between sources take the nearest lower source color, cells above the highest source remain unchanged, and other columns are identical to input.
4. Verify dimensions and row widths before submitting.

Treat this as a task-family hypothesis, not a universal ARC rule; confirm the marker and propagation direction from demos before reuse.

description: Use when nested square/rectangular color bands appear to reverse their layer order.

# Continual-ARC concentric ring reversal

Use when an input contains one or more nested, axis-aligned rectangular/square frames made of uniform-color layers, potentially with a solid center. A demo can indicate that the output preserves each object’s dimensions and geometry but reverses the ordered colors of the concentric layers.

## Evidence and rule
- Represent each object as a sequence of colors from outside to inside: `[c0, c1, ..., ck]`.
- If demos support reversal, recolor the outermost layer with `ck`, the next layer with `c(k-1)`, and so on; the innermost region receives `c0`.
- Apply independently to each nested object, including a uniform filled center as the innermost layer. Preserve background, object boundaries, dimensions, and all coordinates.
- Do not infer a global color substitution: the same color may map differently depending on its layer role/object. This is a positional reversal of each object’s layer sequence.

## Verification
1. Confirm demo input/output boundaries and layer counts match.
2. List each object’s input layer colors outside-in and compare against output outside-in; require exact reversal for every demo object before using the rule.
3. Reconstruct the test output by changing color values only within the matching layers. Keep all background cells unchanged.
4. Check grid dimensions and every row length before submission.

## Demonstrated instance
A demo showed nested objects whose outside-in layer sequences reversed exactly in the output. The held-out test also used differently sized nested objects and solid centers; each object independently followed this reversal. Treat that as evidence for the general operation, not a task-specific color mapping.

# Sparse diagonal structure expansion (task-a61537d7)

Use when a uniform background grid contains sparse 1s and 6s; infer diagonal arms/fields, not generic rays from every marker.

## Demonstration evidence
- Demo 1, 9x9, bg 4: 1s at (2,1),(7,6). Output added 1s along down-right diagonal between them: (3,2),(4,3),(5,4),(6,5). Endpoints retained.
- Demo 2, 8x11, bg 8: 1s at (1,6),(6,1); output added 1s on their anti-diagonal between endpoints: (2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2). A 6 at (3,4) is overwritten as 1. This suggests 1 markers define a straight diagonal segment; segment-fill may overwrite crossing 6s.
- Demo 3, 9x12, bg 4: 1s at (1,7),(7,1); output fills their descending anti-diagonal, rows 2..6 at cols 6..2. A 6 at (6,7) remains unchanged, not on the line.
- Demo 4, 15x12, bg 5: 1s at (3,1),(9,7), aligned down-right; output extends/fills their same diagonal line both directions to grid edges, including cells on the line. 6s also appear as diagonal patterns, but not every 6 is extended into all available rays. Observed 6 anchors at (2,9),(5,3),(8,6),(13,4), outputs trace diagonal structures from these alignments; treat exact 6 selection carefully.
- Demo 5, 15x16, bg 8: 1s at (2,2),(3,12),(11,11),(14,3). Outputs connect the first and last 1s down-right from (2,2) through (14,14), filling intermediate diagonal cells; other 1 anchors remain. 6s at (1,8),(9,9),(10,1),(14,13) produce various diagonal runs: the 6 at (9,9) connects diagonally up-right to (1,1), marking (8,10)..(2,16?) clipped at c=15; the 6 at (10,1) extends down-right to (14,5); 6 at (14,13) remains an endpoint. This example indicates diagonal geometry can be formed by linking compatible same-color anchor pairs and extending selected diagonal lines to borders, but exact eligibility is context-dependent.

## Accepted test rule/output insight
Test 19x16 bg4 anchors: 1 at (2,2),(4,14),(10,10),(17,9); 6 at (4,4),(6,6),(7,14),(15,2). Correct result links/extends the main 1 diagonal through (2,2)->(10,10) (cells r2..10,c2..10), and separately the 6 diagonal sequence along r-c=0 around (4,4),(6,6), giving 6 on r=c where unoccupied, while preserving unrelated marks; a second 6-diagonal pattern uses (7,14) and extends up-left along c-r=7 to boundary/compatible set, and the bottom-left singleton (15,2) stays. The accepted grid was:
[[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4],[4,4,1,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,1,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,1,4],[4,4,4,6,4,1,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,6,4,4,4,6,4,1,4,4,4,4,4,4,6,4],[6,4,4,4,6,4,4,4,1,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,1,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,1,4,4,4,4,4],[4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,6,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,1,4,4,4,4,4,4],[4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4,4]]

name: arc-block-compression
description: Use when ARC grids may compress by repeated rectangular blocks. Infer block-to-cell mapping from demos and verify before submitting.
---

# ARC block compression

Use when a demo transforms a large tiled input into a smaller grid, especially when dimensions suggest uniform blocks (for example 24×24 to 8×8 implies 3×3 patches).

## Procedure
1. Calculate the scale factor from input/output dimensions; verify both row and column factors agree.
2. Partition the input into non-overlapping blocks of that size, aligned at the top-left. A block corresponds to the output cell at the same block-row/block-column index.
3. Compare several blocks—including empty-looking and mixed-color blocks—to the demo output. Identify neutral/background colors and whether the output depends on the dominant remaining color, a specific marker, presence, count, or some other statistic.
4. Verify the proposed mapping for every output cell in all available demonstrations. Do not extrapolate from one region or assume that the largest color count is always decisive; establish neutral colors and tie/no-marker behavior explicitly.
5. Apply to the test grid and preserve output dimensions. Double-check transcription and recompute suspicious blocks; a single missed cell can change the winning color.

## Caution
This is a hypothesis class, not a universal rule. Compression may use a different block size, alignment, statistic, or output convention. Demo requests have a cost, so request another only when plausible mappings disagree on the test and a demonstration could discriminate them.

# ARC block compression

Use when a demo transforms a large tiled input into a smaller grid, especially when dimensions suggest uniform blocks (for example 24×24 to 8×8 implies 3×3 patches).

## Procedure
1. Calculate the scale factor from input/output dimensions; verify both row and column factors agree.
2. Partition the input into non-overlapping blocks of that size, aligned at the top-left. A block corresponds to the output cell at the same block-row/block-column index.
3. Compare several blocks—including empty-looking and mixed-color blocks—to demo output. Identify neutral/background colors and whether the output depends on the dominant remaining color, a specific marker, presence, count, or some other statistic.
4. Verify the proposed mapping for every output cell in all available demonstrations. Do not assume the largest color count is decisive; infer neutral colors and tie/no-marker behavior from examples.
5. Apply to the test grid and preserve output dimensions. Double-check transcription and recompute suspicious blocks; a missed foreground cell can change the winning color.

## Confirmed mapping: 3×3 motif compression with neutral background
A recurring variant partitions the input into aligned 3×3 blocks and emits a smaller grid. In two demonstrated Continual-ARC tasks (18×18→6×6 and 9×9→3×3), color 5 was neutral background: each output cell was the most frequent color in that 3×3 block after excluding 5; output 0 when the block contained only 5s. This explained blocks containing colored motifs as well as sparse singleton foreground marks. Verify the neutral color and tie behavior from the current task's demos before applying; do not transfer color 5 or the mapping blindly to a new task. Check every block, especially mixed blocks and blocks with no non-background cells. A separate 15×15→5×5, 24×24→8×8, and 21×21→7×7 task family independently confirmed the same aligned 3×3 rule with neutral color 5: choose the most frequent among all non-5 cells, including 0 (0 is a valid output color, not an automatically ignored background). A 27×27→9×9 demo and its 15×15→5×5 test independently confirmed this mapping again, with the test solved correctly by per-block mode after excluding 5. This provides strong cross-size evidence for the rule, but still verify block alignment, neutral color, and ties from each task's examples. A corrected 21×21 solve also highlighted the need to count each block carefully: a block containing a uniform 7 region outputs 7, while the adjacent block with four 3s among non-5 cells outputs 3. Use a small per-block frequency tally rather than visual impression.

## Caution
This is a hypothesis class, not a universal rule. Compression may use a different block size, alignment, statistic, or output convention. Request another demo only when plausible mappings disagree on the test and a demonstration could discriminate them.

# ARC demo selection

Use this class-level guide when a puzzle interface charges for demonstrations or provides a limited demo budget. Follow the task-specific skill for the response format and solve procedure.

## Information-value workflow

1. State at least two candidate rules that explain the examples so far.
2. Find a concrete input feature on which those candidates predict different outputs.
3. Request a demo only if it can plausibly expose that distinction and the information is worth its cost. Prefer structural variation (geometry, marker positions, palette, orientation, scale) over a near-duplicate that only repeats an already-supported case.
4. After each demo, test the complete rule against all examples. Distinguish directly observed behavior from assumptions.
5. Stop requesting once the rule yields a determinate prediction for the test. Apply it, validate dimensions and cell values, and submit rather than spending remaining demo budget by default.
6. If a demo does not separate the hypotheses, reassess whether another request is likely to help; do not request repeatedly without identifying its expected information gain.

## Pitfalls

- Similar demos can confirm a visible pattern without identifying its trigger. Seek a case where candidate rules disagree, not merely another example of the same geometry.
- A large remaining budget is not a reason to consume it. Each request is a scored cost; balance information gain against submitting the best-supported rule.
- If all plausible candidates give the same test grid, submit it instead of seeking unnecessary certainty.

## Relationship to ARC skills

`arc-reasoning` provides the general evidence-first puzzle workflow; `continual-arc` provides the constrained action contract. This skill focuses on the information-value decision of whether to request additional examples.

# Selecting demonstrations for ambiguous component recoloring

In selective recoloring tasks, multiple same-colored connected components may coexist, but only one is changed to a guide object's color. Seeing one changed component in an example does not itself reveal how the component is selected or how the guide color is chosen. Before paying for another demo, enumerate plausible rules (such as relative size, position, shape, proximity, or alignment) and identify a concrete observation that would cause them to predict different transformations. Prefer structurally discriminating demos over more examples that only repeat the broad pattern. A sequence of demos with diverse colors/shapes can still fail to reveal the selector; mark the rule unresolved and avoid submitting a speculative component selection. Apply this note alongside the general information-value workflow in `arc-demo-selection/SKILL.md`.

# task-40f9faf7: eight-demo recurrence (test prediction rejected)

This is evidence from a single recurrence, not a confirmed universal rule. Test grid was 18×28 on background 4 with numerous separated components in colors 2, 5, 6, 7, 9. Eight demos showed that only one component changed in each output, and the new color was often the color of another shape resembling or containing it. Crucially, all eight demonstrations were spent without determining the exact selector, and the test submission recoloring the top 9 component to 3 was rejected. Do not treat that prediction as accepted.

Selected demo diffs:
- Demo 1 (11×16): component 7 at rows 2–3, cols 7–10 changed to 9; a 9 line/object exists elsewhere. Other 7 component at lower right remains.
- Demo 2 (12×13): two 1s at (10,4),(11,5) changed to 5, matching the color of a vertical 5 object elsewhere; other components unchanged.
- Demo 3 (20×11): two 5s at (14,5),(15,5) changed to 9; a 9-colored horizontal/irregular object is elsewhere.
- Demo 4 (19×13): the 8 rectangle at rows 2–6, cols 7–8 changed to 9, while another 8 outlier remained; the replacement color matches a separate 9 component.
- Demo 5 (27×17): two 6s at (10,3),(11,3) changed to 1; another component in color 6 remained unchanged.
- Demo 6 (18×22): a 5 pair at rows 3–4, col 19 changed to 9; unrelated 5 objects remained.
- Demo 7 (29×24): the 5×5 9 component at rows 19–23, cols 0–4 changed to 3; other 9 components remained.
- Demo 8 (28×21): singleton 9 at (2,2) changed to 5; other 9 regions remained.

The target test contains a 9 singleton at (0,18), a vertical 9 run at rows 0–4,col18, and a 2×2 9 component at rows 4–5, cols 18–19; the previously submitted guess changed that latter 2×2 component to 3 and was rejected. The test also has 5 block-like objects, 6 components, 7 components, and a 2 vertical component. Since binary feedback only says some part of the predicted grid was wrong, it does not identify whether the selected component, target color, shape correspondence, or transcription was mistaken. No accurate result was confirmed in the current recurrence.

Reusable caution: single-component recoloring is selective, not a global mapping. Demos suggest shape relations to guide objects may matter, but the exact relation needs a genuinely discriminating example. Do not spend the full demo budget merely accumulating examples of “some object changes”; after each, compare candidate selectors (shape equality/subshape, size, orientation, enclosure, position) against every changed and preserved component. If the test output is still not uniquely determined, preserve uncertainty rather than calling an intuitive match confirmed.

# Continual-ARC demo selection: task-8958825c

This interaction illustrates a budget pitfall, not a solved transformation. After receiving two demo pairs, the solver requested a third without stating competing hypotheses, an input feature that would separate them, or how the third example could alter the held-out prediction. The evidence at that point was insufficient to infer the grid transformation, and no output was submitted; do not treat this as a solved rule or infer an answer from the demos alone.

For a task with a charged, capped demo budget, keep a compact live ledger after each pair: identify changed regions/cells and preserved structure, name at least two candidate transformations, compute their test predictions, and record the exact remaining budget. Request another pair only when you can say what observation in it would distinguish candidates and why that distinction matters for the test. If no such discriminating query is identifiable, weigh the best-supported submission against the request cost rather than spending demos reflexively. After every response, re-read the updated counts before taking the next action.

---
name: arc-guided-translation
description: Use when a guide line may imply motif translation.
---

# ARC guide-directed motif translation

Use when an ARC grid contains a full-length straight guide (often a distinctive line color) and a separate patterned region nearby. Do not assume the output merely adds a stripe: the motif may move toward the guide while a full-length stripe fills the vacated boundary.

## Evidence-first workflow

1. Identify the guide orientation/location, background color, patterned region, and any other marks. Preserve exact input coordinates.
2. Compare every demo cell-by-cell. Determine whether the guide persists; whether the motif moves, changes shape, or stays fixed; the displacement direction/magnitude; and what color fills vacated cells. Compare the motif as a whole rather than only noticing newly added stripes.
3. For the translation candidate, map all motif cells under a single displacement vector. Check that the output motif has the same shape/colors at shifted coordinates, except for any explicitly demonstrated changes. Determine whether the vacated boundary receives a full-length stripe, only a local fill, or background.
4. Verify the rule against every demo, including preserved cells and boundaries. Do not extrapolate a fixed stripe coordinate or displacement unless examples support it.
5. Apply to the test only when displacement and stripe behavior are supported. Check interactions with the guide, clipping, output dimensions, and every changed cell. If candidate directions or scope remain ambiguous, request a discriminating demo rather than submit a stripe-only guess.

## Confirmed recurring variant

Two demonstrations showed a patterned motif adjacent to a full-length color-2 guide. With a vertical guide to the right, the motif shifted one cell right and a full-length color-8 stripe occupied the vacated leftmost motif column. With a horizontal guide below, the motif shifted one cell down and a full-length color-8 stripe occupied the vacated top row. The guide and all unrelated cells remained unchanged. Thus the tested variant is one-cell translation toward the guide plus a color-8 line at the vacated edge, not stripe addition alone. Infer colors, distance, and exact stripe scope from current-task examples rather than transferring blindly.

## Pitfalls

- A correct stripe with an unmoved object is still an incorrect transformation when the stripe marks the object's vacated boundary.
- Broadly recoloring a whole grid row/column can be wrong if demos show only the vacated motif boundary; distinguish the stripe's scope from its position.
- Sparse or irregular motifs are easy to transcribe incorrectly. Verify the translated foreground cell-by-cell, preserving holes and unrelated marks.
- Binary incorrect feedback does not localize a missed movement, stripe endpoint, color, or transcription error. Do not repeat the same stripe-only output; revisit the full delta and request an informative demo if needed.

---
name: arc-pattern-inference
description: Use when ARC grids have ambiguous geometric cues.
---

# ARC geometric pattern inference

Use for ARC tasks where isolated marks, border-attached runs, aligned cells, or scattered shapes may encode a geometric transformation. This class-level workflow complements general ARC reasoning by emphasizing complete difference analysis and discrimination among competing spatial rules. For an ambiguous Continual-ARC instance with edge-connected runs and interior marks, see `references/edge-seeded-grid-patterns.md` for a concrete cautionary case; its exact transformation remains unverified.

## Workflow

1. **Map each demo exactly.** Record dimensions, background candidates, edge-connected runs, interior objects, and every changed coordinate. Preserve an immutable copy of each input while comparing.
2. **Separate evidence from interpretation.** Note which structures are copied, extended, recolored, erased, or untouched. Do not assume every unusual cell is an anchor, every aligned pair is active, or every edge run participates.
3. **Construct competing rules.** For example, distinguish extending from a singleton versus from a pair, filling an entire line versus only a bounded segment, and treating a border run as a seed versus as an invariant. State where these rules predict different cells.
4. **Test all demos.** Reject any candidate that fails to explain even one changed or preserved feature. Favor the simplest complete rule, not the most visually compelling local pattern.
5. **Choose informative evidence.** If candidates remain and another example is affordable, request a demo whose geometry, orientation, or edge placement makes their predictions differ. A near-duplicate that only repeats known behavior has lower information value.
6. **Apply conservatively.** Change only cells licensed by the demonstrated rule, preserve unrelated marks, and verify dimensions, row lengths, and values before submission.
7. **Treat binary rejection as nonlocalizing.** Reassess rule scope, trigger, direction, and cell transcription; do not cycle through cosmetic variants without new evidence.

## Pitfalls

- One demo may show an expansion without identifying whether its trigger is color, edge contact, alignment, or another spatial condition.
- A visible run can be a boundary condition rather than a seed. Verify against examples with different orientations or locations.
- A broad speculative fill is especially risky when sparse markers and edge-attached shapes coexist; use discriminating demos rather than overextending a local pattern.
- In constrained-action environments, reasoning must end in exactly one permitted action. Do not call unrelated tools to inspect or calculate puzzle grids after the required task guidance has been loaded.

# Invalid grid feedback and uncertain line-extension rules

This note captures two reusable lessons from a noisy-grid Continual-ARC attempt.

## Invalid-output recovery
When feedback explicitly says a submission was not a valid ARC grid, first distinguish a serialization/shape problem from a semantic miss. Before resubmitting, validate JSON syntax, exactly the expected number of rows, uniform row widths, and integer cell values in range 0–9. A semantically correct idea cannot be assessed until the grid is valid; do not use invalid-grid feedback to revise the transformation rule.

## Ambiguous center-line extensions
Large monochrome square patches can tempt an inference that their center rows and columns extend across the entire canvas. This is only a hypothesis until demos establish the behavior at existing non-background cells and other patches. Track whether the proposed lines overwrite, preserve, stop at, or skip pre-existing cells, and account for line intersections. Compare candidate outputs explicitly and request a discriminating demo if affordable. Do not burn submissions on small coordinate adjustments to an unverified global-line hypothesis.

The lesson is methodological, not a confirmed transform for any particular task.

# Demo-turn discipline in constrained ARC puzzles

Every returned demonstration is new evidence; do not treat it as a cue to request another automatically. Compare the example's input and output, noting changed and preserved cells, transformations, dimensions, and colors. Update the candidate rules and the prediction for the test before taking another action.

Before a paid demo request, specify the competing hypotheses and the concrete observation that would distinguish them. If no plausible demo can resolve a named uncertainty, stop spending requests and decide whether the most conservative supported output merits submission. Additional demonstrations do not validate a rule merely by accumulating; varied but non-discriminating examples can leave the task unresolved.

In strict one-action interfaces, puzzle turns should contain only the permitted action. Once task-relevant guidance is loaded, avoid repeated skill/reference calls between turns; reason from the actual evidence and choose one action.

# Edge-seeded grid patterns: unresolved example and method

One Continual-ARC task (task-722587bd) had 23×17, 8×27, 12×11, 24×26, 18×21, and 21×6 examples with uniform fields, short edge-attached runs, and sparse interior cells. Outputs preserved dimensions and often expanded or recolored interior cells while leaving some edge-attached runs unchanged. In several demos, 1-marked areas expanded to regions; in another, a 0 mark turned into a 4 while a larger 0 region appeared; another produced a long 0 strip from a 0 seed aligned with an edge-attached 1 pair. Despite the variety, the five demos did not establish a sufficiently precise deterministic rule for the test.

The test had background 3, 6-runs on the top-right and bottom-left edges, and 1 singletons at (5,7), (18,9), and (20,8), zero-based. A speculative output expanded edge-related 1 areas and singleton-derived fills, but the transcript ended before correctness feedback. Therefore that prediction and any inferred mapping of edge runs to regions are UNVERIFIED; do not treat the precise test fill as a reusable rule.

For a recurrence, enumerate all demo diffs rather than relying on a single plausible geometric story. Check whether transformations depend on edge-run length/orientation, relative location of singleton markers, row/column alignment, or the region between an edge feature and an interior seed. Seek a demo where those candidate rules yield different changes. After a speculative submission, binary feedback (if received) cannot identify the offending cells: require new evidence or a genuinely revised, demo-supported hypothesis.

# Learning from rejected ARC submissions

A binary incorrect result says only that the submitted grid is not exact; it does not identify the wrong cell or validate any unchanged part of the hypothesis. Repeated submissions that reproduce the same output—or toggle a few cells without a new deduction—burn attempt budget without gaining information.

Before another submission:

1. Preserve the prior candidate grid or its concise changed-coordinate list.
2. Compare the proposed candidate with the last rejected candidate. Do not resubmit an identical grid.
3. For every changed coordinate, name the new demo evidence or structural deduction that warrants the change. If there is none, do not submit the variant.
4. Replay the full proposed rule against every demo, checking both changed and preserved cells exactly.
5. If plausible rules still predict different test outputs, use an affordable demo to discriminate rather than cycling through guesses. Once the demo budget is exhausted, make one deliberate best-supported prediction, not a sequence of repeated speculative grids.

This applies especially to large grids where manual transcription can accidentally make successive grids identical or nearly identical. Keep the transformation simple, use row/column indexing carefully, and validate the output dimensions and all rule-driven coordinates before submission.

# Selective line-span fills in sparse-marker grids

Some marker/fill tasks operate in both orientations but do not fill every line with multiple markers. A demonstrated selective variant qualifies a row or column only when its marker positions include an adjacent pair (a contiguous marker run of length ≥2); on a qualifying line, background cells strictly between the outermost markers are filled, while marker cells and outside cells are preserved. The output is the union of qualifying horizontal and vertical spans.

Do not transfer this predicate blindly: establish line eligibility, orientation, colors, and span endpoints from the current task's demonstrations. Ordinary horizontal-only tasks may instead qualify every row with at least two markers. Conversely, singletons or several separated markers may remain untouched in the selective 2D variant.

## Validation checklist

1. For every demo, record marker positions per row and per column, identify contiguous marker runs, and compare output changes with qualifying spans.
2. Check unmodified gaps explicitly; these can falsify a rule that fills all intervals between markers.
3. For a test prediction, list qualifying rows and columns before filling. Compute the union of their spans, preserving markers and all unrelated cells.
4. After a rejected answer, consider both a rule error and an incomplete/manual transcription. Do not make a small unsupported edit and retry; use a discriminating demo when the rule remains uncertain.
5. Validate every row length, grid dimensions, and that each changed cell belongs to a demonstrated span.

This note records a candidate rule family, not a universal transformation. A previous instance with the same task label had contradictory outcomes in stored records; rely on the active instance's actual demos rather than historical guessed outputs.

# Sequential demo use in Continual-ARC

A returned pair is evidence to analyze, not merely a reason to request another pair. Immediately compare the pair cell by cell: identify invariant structure, changed coordinates, colors and geometry; then revise the candidate rule set and the predicted test output.

Before paying for another demo, articulate the live alternatives and what specific output/input distinction would separate them. A demo is valuable when its geometry, orientation, dimensions, or color arrangement makes candidate predictions diverge. Avoid serial requests without incorporating each result. If examples vary substantially but leave the rule underdetermined, stop requesting passively and submit the best-supported conservative prediction while budget remains.

This discipline matters especially when demos seem unrelated at first glance: compare transformations rather than surface shapes. Look for invariant operations (e.g. moving a foreground object and laying a distinct-color line along the newly vacated coordinate), test them across every example, and apply to the test only after validating the exact direction and preserved cells.

# Shape validation before Continual-ARC submission

A submitted grid can be rejected as invalid before the transformation is evaluated if its dimensions do not match the required output. In a recent 19×16 test, two hand-written predictions accidentally had 18 rows; both were structurally invalid, independent of the rule hypothesis.

For same-size outputs, before submitting:
1. Count rows and ensure the count equals the required height.
2. Count cells in every row; each must equal required width.
3. Verify every value is an integer in 0–9.
4. Recheck every edit against the inferred operation and preserve unaffected cells.

Long nested arrays are prone to omitted rows. Prefer a row-by-row checklist or generated grid where tools are allowed; in a strict one-action turn, manually enumerate and count rows. Structural validity is separate from semantic correctness.

# Sparse singleton expansion: unresolved review (task-90835804)

Two demos showed a 1×N row with a centered single color-2 marker expanded into an N×N grid. For N=5, color 2 formed a symmetric downward fan to full width by row 2; color 1 appeared in two isolated lower cells. For N=13, color 2 formed the analogous fan to full width by row 6; color 1 then occupied a slanted/repeating lower pattern. This supports the fan and existence of a second color-1 structure, but not the exact continuation rule or extrapolation to width 17.

Two rejected test predictions used the same color-2 fan through width 17, then a period-4 color-1 pattern; the only change between attempts was the color-1 phase. Both failed. Do not retry either phase or treat period 4 as validated. The rejection could concern the fan boundary, lower pattern, phase, or other detail. If a demo remains, request it to distinguish candidate lower-continuation rules before guessing again. In general, isolate the region directly supported by demos from an uncertain continuation, and do not make cosmetic phase changes after binary rejection.

name: arc-prototype-stamping
description: Use when a puzzle has one multicolor prototype and isolated markers that may trigger copies.
---

# Prototype stamping at isolated markers

Use when an ARC grid contains a distinctive non-background shape and separate isolated cells that may indicate where to replicate it.

## Inference workflow
1. Identify background, the putative prototype shape, and isolated trigger cells by color/connectivity.
2. Compare input and output: check whether the prototype remains and copies appear at marker positions.
3. Infer the anchor from the examples. A common rule centers the prototype's bounding box on each marker (including even-width/height tie direction, if relevant); another rule may align a particular prototype cell to the marker. Do not assume which without evidence.
4. Verify translated copies at every trigger, including whether markers are overwritten, whether copies preserve all prototype colors including any background-colored holes, and how overlap/clipping is handled.
5. Apply the demonstrated transform to all markers, preserve unaffected cells and grid dimensions, and validate against all demos.

## Observed Continual-ARC case
Task `task-714f81c9` had background 8, a 1×5 motif `[2,1,2,2,6]`, and isolated 3 markers. The single demo used a 3×3 multicolor motif with isolated 7 markers. Each marker was replaced by a translated copy of the full motif, with the motif's bounding-box center aligned to the marker; the original motif remained. Thus in the 1×5 case, the center (third) motif cell aligns with each marker. This is one demonstrated rule, not a universal ARC assumption; infer independently from each task's examples.

Replicate the entire template at each trigger, aligning the template's bounding-box center to the trigger. The trigger is overwritten by the template's center cell; preserve the original prototype. For odd-sized templates, the center is unambiguous. Examples include a 1×5 horizontal motif (center index 2), a 3×1 vertical motif (center index 1), and a 3×3 motif whose top row is background except for a central distinctive color. The latter shows why the template must include the distinctive padding cell, not only the dense adjacent shape. An additional resolved test used a 3×3 two-color prototype with a separate single-cell trigger; the copy's bounding-box center aligned exactly with the trigger and the original prototype remained unchanged. Index carefully: for a 3×3 prototype centered on a zero-based trigger (r,c), stamp rows r−1..r+1 and columns c−1..c+1. A one-row-up placement that instead starts at r−2 is wrong; confirm that the trigger coordinate receives the prototype’s center cell. Another confirmed recurrence of task−714f81c9 used a 1×5 prototype `[9,9,9,3,4]` on background 5, with isolated 8s as triggers. Keep the entire five-cell motif intact and center it on each 8 (so the center 9 overwrites the trigger); preserve the original motif. This generalizes the motif length in that task, not the specific colors. A further confirmed recurrence of task-714f81c9 had background 7, a 5×5 irregular multicolor prototype at rows 6–10/columns 1–5, and an isolated 9 trigger at (row 2, column 5). The full prototype bounding box (including background-valued cells) was centered on the trigger; the template center replaced the 9, the original stayed intact, and the copy used offset (−6,+2).

---
name: arc-reasoning
description: Use for ARC-style puzzles. Test rules against all examples.
---

# ARC-style puzzle reasoning

Use this class-level workflow for ARC grid transformations, including continual task streams. Follow the task-specific protocol and output contract in any more specialized skill.

## Evidence-first solving

1. Parse dimensions, colors, budgets, and interaction protocol. Treat each task as independent.
2. Compare each demo input and output at the cell level. Record changed cells and unchanged boundaries, then infer color roles, direction, scope, and eligibility conditions.
3. Keep candidate rules that explain every demo, but distinguish observed facts from untested assumptions. A simple explanation fitting a demo is not necessarily uniquely identified.
4. For each candidate, predict the test output. Identify cells on which the candidates disagree. Ask whether the demos actually test that distinction; if not, request a discriminating example when its information value justifies the cost.
5. Apply the best-supported rule while preserving unaffected cells. Validate output dimensions, row lengths, and cell values.
6. After an incorrect submission, treat feedback as evidence that some detail is wrong. Revisit scope, direction, color, and eligibility rather than repeating the same output. Submit again only when a concrete new deduction supports the change; prioritize informative demos over repeated guesses when the rule remains underdetermined.

## Confirmed pattern: lattice compression / 3×3 macrotiles

Some noisy ARC grids compress by treating each aligned 3×3 block as one macrocell; output dimensions are input dimensions divided by 3 (e.g. 21×21→7×7, 12×12→4×4, 15×15→5×5). In a demonstrated task, each output macrocell carried a color associated with the salient coherent motif in that 3×3 input tile, with 0 for tiles without a qualifying motif. Test solved correctly with a 5×5 output. Do not infer that the answer is always the majority color: demo tiles can output a minority color (e.g. three 3s in a tile otherwise 5, and two 6s in a tile otherwise 5), while other tiles output a majority/singleton pattern color. Examine local arrangements and motifs; preserve 0 as meaningful output/background. Confirm block alignment from dimensions and demos, and validate every tile separately. This family is related to compression but distinct from the rectangular/special-line sampling rule below.

## Confirmed pattern: periodic-lattice compression

In one Continual-ARC task, a large grid with repeated rectangular regions and regularly spaced special rows/columns compressed to a small matrix with one cell per macro region. Demo output sizes varied, confirming output dimensions follow macro-region counts rather than raw input dimensions. Sparse marks on special lines contributed selectively; the exact per-cell mapping was not reducible to copying all intersections or one chosen line. Accepted 25×11 test output was `[[0,7,7],[0,0,0],[7,0,8]]`. Treat this as a candidate family: identify macro cells and infer mapping from demos; do not assume a universal sampling rule.

## Pitfalls

A demo showing color changes only after a marker may fit both “recolor the suffix” and “recolor every background cell in a marker-containing row.” It does not distinguish those rules if there is no background before the marker. Do not treat the narrower visual pattern as confirmed without a case that separates them.

For Continual-ARC's exact action syntax and score accounting, consult the `continual-arc` skill.

# Continual-ARC horizontal-band / vertical-gap-column completion

Use when a grid has sparse horizontal colored bars, typically anchored on the left and/or right edge, plus vertical colored bars or markers. A horizontal band's internal one-cell gaps identify vertical tracks. Multiple horizontal bands share tracks, and the track color changes at each band level. Do not interpret as ordinary horizontal gap-fill alone.

## Evidence-supported model
Across three demos for task-0879ec47, each horizontal band has a gap column where its color switches/starts around a vertical track. Fill each such gap with the band color. Extend that track vertically in the same color through the vertical interval associated with that band: from the prior band's row (exclusive) through this band's row, or from the grid edge if it is the first band. At the next horizontal band, the track switches to that band's color. Where lower vertical source-bars of a different color occur, preserve them and their cells; demo 1/2 show these bottom bars defining the lower segment color below the final horizontal band. Some bottom isolated marks may remain untouched; do not extend them unless demos establish a matching lower continuation.

### Exact observed checks
- Demo 1: row 9 has a left color-2 bar with gap column 3 and right color-3 bar/track at column 9. Output fills row-9 gaps and extends color 2 in column 3 over rows 0–9, color 3 in column 9 over rows 0–9. Lower original vertical bars remain (column 3 color 3 from row 10; column 9 color 4 from row 10).
- Demo 2: horizontal bands at rows 3 (color 3, gap/track c3), 6 (color 6, track c9), and 8 (color 4 at c3 / color 7 at c9). Output uses c3 color 3 rows 0–3, color 4 rows 4–8; c9 color 6 rows 0–6, color 7 rows 7–8. Bottom source bars c3=1 and c9=5 stay intact from rows 9/11 down.
- Demo 3: tracks c1 and c9 switch color at successive horizontal bands (rows 2,3,5,8,11); their outputs form vertically contiguous color bands between horizontal rows. Bottom row marks at c1 and c9 extend color 1 upward over rows 12–14.

## Application and caution
1. Identify every horizontal band and its internal gap/track columns; preserve the original colored bars.
2. For each track, order the band rows and assign each vertical interval the color specified by its corresponding band's adjacent horizontal bar. Fill the one-cell gaps in horizontal bands as observed.
3. Respect existing lower vertical bars and boundaries. A track can be sourced by a bottom bar/marker as well as by horizontal bands, but only propagate bottom colors when the demos show that matching arrangement.
4. Validate all demos cell by cell, especially track transitions and unchanged bottom regions, before applying. Similar-looking irregular edge bars can encode more complicated interactions; binary feedback is not localizing.

For task-0879ec47, the accepted 15×15 test had horizontal bands at rows 2/3/6/8/11, tracks c3 and c8, with color sequences on c3: 2 (rows 0–2), 3 (rows 3–6), 4 (rows 7–11); on c8: 5 (rows 0–3), 9 (rows 4–8), 4 (rows 9–11). Original bottom marks at c3/c8 rows 13–14 were preserved. The accepted output also filled the internal horizontal gaps at the corresponding bands. This accepted case confirms these exact bands/track transitions, not a universal rule for all edge-bar grids.

# Sparse diagonal structures (task-a61537d7)

Use when a uniform-background grid contains sparse 1 and 6 marks and diagonal segments/runs are implied. Do not treat every isolated mark as a generic ray; infer aligned diagonals and preserve unrelated cells.

## Demonstrations
- Demo 1 (9x9, bg4): 1 at (2,1),(7,6); output fills the down-right diagonal between them with 1s.
- Demo 2 (8x11, bg8): 1 at (1,6),(6,1); output fills intervening anti-diagonal cells; a 6 on the line is overwritten by 1.
- Demo 3 (9x12, bg4): 1 at (1,7),(7,1); output fills intervening anti-diagonal. An off-line 6 remains unchanged.
- Demo 4 (15x12, bg5): 1 at (3,1),(9,7); output fills and extends that down-right diagonal to both grid edges. 6 marks participate in selected diagonal alignments, but not every 6 marker is extended as an unrestricted ray.
- Demo 5 (15x16, bg8): 1 at (2,2),(14,3) form a main down-right line; output fills its full diagonal. Other 1s at (3,12),(11,11) remain. Several 6s form selectively completed diagonal lines; the precise selector is context-sensitive.

## Accepted test
For the 19x16 bg4 test, 1s at (2,2),(10,10) produce a down-right diagonal segment (including both anchors), and other 1s stay unchanged. Diagonal 6 structures include runs on aligned down-right/up-right trajectories; some mark rays extend to edges, while unrelated 6 at (15,2) stays isolated. Accepted output exactly:

# Divider-separated mask transformation

For Continual-ARC tasks where a full-width solid 7 row separates an upper binary panel (0/1) from a lower panel (0/4), inspect demonstrations for output mapping.

Confirmed task instance: output keeps only the upper panel height and same width. For every cell in the upper panel, output 2 where the input cell is 1 and the corresponding cell in the lower panel is 0; otherwise output 0. The divider and lower panel are discarded. This is a cellwise coincidence between a top sparse mask and bottom holes (lower 0s), encoded as color 2. Confirm with demos before reuse; this is a task family clue, not a universal ARC rule.

Example evidence: a 6×26 upper region and 6×26 lower region separated by a row of 7 produced a 6×26 result. For the 15×6 example, the sparse ones had no coincident holes underneath, so output was all zero. Test case with four upper rows and four lower rows yielded 4×4 output.

Workflow: identify full separator row, determine output crop dimensions, align top and bottom panels, infer whether output depends on foreground coincidence or inverse holes, and check all demo cells before submitting. Preserve 0s elsewhere.

name: continual-arc-divider-mask-copy
description: Use for two panels separated by a solid 7 row.

# Divider-separated panel overlap / mask transform

For a grid split into two equal-sized panels by a solid divider (orientation and divider color vary), align corresponding panel coordinates and infer which cell values denote active/non-background cells from the demos. A supported recurring rule is to emit color 2 where BOTH aligned cells are nonzero, otherwise 0; discard the divider and return a grid with the panel dimensions. Do not assume 0/1 polarity or treat the dominant color as background automatically: in examples, zero was the sparse inactive value even when another color was numerically/density-dominant. Verify the predicate and output color from the current task's demos.

Evidence across instances: a horizontal divider separated binary/random panels and output retained the panel-sized top height. One 21×15 example used upper-panel background 8 and lower-panel background 1, with zero-valued holes; output 2 occurred where both aligned inputs were nonzero. A second 11×24 example used sparse zeros against colors 6 and 3; output 2 likewise marked positions where both aligned inputs were nonzero. A vertical-divider instance with a 22×9 input used a solid color-5 column, two 22×4 panels, and sparse 6 markers in the right panel; the 22×4 output was 2 exactly where a right-side 6 aligned with a left-side 1, otherwise 0.

Workflow: find the full solid divider; crop the two equal panels on either side; align coordinates; infer active values/predicate and output color from every demo; compute output at panel dimensions and validate cellwise. For confirmed nonzero-coincidence tasks, calculate each output cell explicitly as 2 iff both aligned panel values are nonzero, otherwise 0. A common failure mode is a few hand-transcribed cells/rows or a one-row indexing slip; verify every output row against the corresponding input rows on both sides of the divider, including the first and last panel rows. Related tasks may instead use coincidence of holes or another mask relation, so never transfer a predicate solely from the divider shape.

Additional confirmed variant: in three demos with a horizontal solid divider, differently colored dense panels (foreground 5/8 or 3/4) and sparse zeros, output 2 exactly at aligned coordinates where BOTH panel cells are nonzero; zeros in either panel suppress the output. This establishes that the mask is occupancy/nonzero coincidence—not coincidence of holes, nor a requirement that panel colors match. Infer this polarity from examples; a visually dense color can be active even when the panels have different colors.

Further confirmation: a 29×18 input with a full-width color-8 divider at row 15, upper 14×18 panel of 5s/0s and lower 14×18 panel of 4s/0s produced a 14×18 output of 2 iff both aligned cells were nonzero, otherwise 0. A 30×9 vertical-divider instance with a full-height color-6 separator, left 30×4 panel of 3s with occasional zeros, and right 30×4 panel of 1s/0s confirmed the same rule: output shape 30×4 and value 2 iff both cells are nonzero. For large grids, compute the cellwise mask programmatically and verify panel boundaries/dimensions rather than hand-transcribing output rows; manual row/cell errors can burn attempts despite the rule being correct.

Another confirmed vertical-divider example: input shape 14×23 with a full-height color-1 divider at column 12, yielding two 14×11 panels. The left panel was mostly color 8 with a few zero holes; the right panel was mostly color 9 with scattered zeros. Output was 14×11, with color 2 exactly where both aligned cells were nonzero, and 0 wherever either side was zero. This further confirms that unequal background colors and sparse holes do not alter the nonzero-coincidence rule; preserve panel order/alignment and exclude the separator.

name: continual-arc-divider-union-mask
description: Use when a divider separates binary masks that combine by union. For this task family, OR the active cells across aligned panels and emit 3.

# Divider-separated binary-mask union

For confirmed task `task-4da17d3f`, a 9×5 input has a solid horizontal color-4 divider at row 5, separating two aligned 4×5 panels. The upper panel uses 2 as active and 0 as inactive; the lower panel uses 1 as active and 0 as inactive. Output is a 4×5 grid where each cell is 3 iff either aligned panel cell is nonzero; otherwise 0:

`out[r][c] = 3 if (top[r][c] != 0 or bottom[r][c] != 0) else 0`.

This is a UNION/OR mask, not an intersection: a single active value in either panel suffices. Discard the divider, preserve row/column alignment, and output color 3. Validate the complete panel dimensions and all cells. This rule was confirmed against a demo and correctly applied to the test input; do not transfer it to other divider tasks without checking their demonstrations because divider tasks may use different predicates/colors.

Example demonstrated test output:
`[[0,3,3,3,3],[0,0,0,3,3],[3,3,0,3,3],[3,3,3,0,3]]`.

Demo confirms union behavior: output marks the union of the upper 2-mask and lower 1-mask, with zero where both aligned cells are zero.

name: continual-arc-evidence-ledger
description: Use when Continual-ARC demos arrive sequentially.
---

# Sequential demo evidence ledger for Continual-ARC

Use alongside `continual-arc` and `arc-demo-selection` when solving a demo-limited Continual-ARC task. This is a process aid, not a transformation rule.

## Maintain a live ledger
After each demo arrives, before choosing the next action:
1. Note input/output dimensions and palette/background candidates.
2. List every changed output cell or region and its input value; separately note meaningful preserved examples/counterexamples.
3. Record current candidate rules, what each explains, and the unresolved distinction.
4. Recompute the held-out test prediction under each live candidate. For dimensionality-changing tasks, explicitly derive the output coordinate system and mapping from input structure to output cells; do not hand-guess coordinates from visual resemblance.

## Spend demos deliberately
Before each additional `request_demos`, identify at least two live hypotheses and one concrete property of a future example that would make their predictions diverge. If the prior demo did not update or narrow the candidates, do not request the next one automatically. Prefer an informative request when an actionable distinction is plausible; stop requesting if more examples are unlikely to resolve it and select the best-supported action under the cost model.

## Recover from rejection
Binary incorrect feedback rejects at least one part of the entire prediction and does not localize the error. Revisit the whole rule (scope, selector, coordinate encoding, colors, and transcription). Do not submit cosmetic variants or toggle isolated cells without new evidence. A new submission should follow from a materially revised, demo-supported hypothesis and be checked for dimensions and row lengths.

## Scope and caution
A fixed output shape across differently sized inputs is strong evidence to investigate compression or feature encoding, but does not specify the encoding. Infer it from all examples. Repeated similar demonstrations are not proof that an unresolved selector or mapping is identified. Do not claim an answer where examples leave the transform unresolved.

# Continual-ARC action-turn discipline

The puzzle interface is a strict one-action-per-turn protocol. For each puzzle message, perform only the reasoning needed to select exactly one permitted action (`submit`, `request_demos`, or, once complete, `finish`) and make that the final-line JSON response. Do not issue auxiliary shell/terminal calls, unrelated skill lookups, or prose during the puzzle instance; these do not help infer the transformation and risk violating the output contract.

When a demo arrives, compare its input and output cellwise, update the live hypotheses, and recompute the test prediction before deciding whether to request another demo or submit. Spend a demo only when the next example could distinguish live candidate rules; do not request simply because budget remains.

# Inferring coordinate mappings in geometric rearrangements

Use this note when demonstrations establish that multiple colored components are rearranged but do not make the precise packing rule obvious.

## Procedure
1. Segment the input into objects/components and record each object's color, bounding box, exact footprint, size, and relative order.
2. For each demo, record the output bounding box and anchor coordinate of every corresponding object. Do not confuse identifying which objects move with identifying where they move.
3. Compare candidate coordinate rules: whole-grid rotation/reflection/translation; independent object translation; compact row/column packing; staircase/diagonal placement; anchors determined by source location, object dimensions, ordering, or cumulative preceding-object size.
4. Test each candidate against every component, including unchanged objects, and calculate the held-out prediction explicitly. Check cell counts and shapes are preserved unless demos show edits.
5. If candidates disagree on the held-out output and a demo remains, request an example varying the disputed feature (e.g. object dimensions, order, or source location). Do not extrapolate destinations from visual resemblance alone.

## Case-study caution
Two 10×10 demonstrations showed several solid rectangular color blocks originally aligned along the lower edge being moved into an upper-left staircase-like composition. The broad fact of rearrangement was visible, but the examples did not uniquely establish how all destination anchors were determined. A test submission assembled by visually shifting the components was not validated. Treat that as evidence of an under-specified mapping, not as a known transform or answer key. The reusable lesson is to derive and verify object-to-anchor correspondence before submitting.

## Verification checklist
- Every original colored component accounted for exactly once.
- Shape, area, color, and internal pattern preserved where supported.
- Output anchors match one consistent rule across demos.
- No unintended overlap; dimensions and row lengths validated.
- Held-out prediction was derived from the rule rather than manually imitated.

# Multi-component contour and fill transformations: unresolved case study

A task instance showed multiple disconnected, color-1 line-art components on a 0 background. Across four demonstrations, selected components gained a color-2 outer contour/background extension and color-3 interior fills, while other components remained unchanged. Some altered components had ragged or incomplete boundaries, so a simple rule such as “expand every outline” did not explain the evidence. The fourth demo confirmed a nearby component could remain untouched despite resembling the transformed forms.

The proposed 30×30 test output followed a loose interpretation of those contours, but was rejected. This does not localize the error; do not treat any attempted coordinate/color assignment here as a validated answer.

Reusable lessons:
- Segment disconnected components before inferring a transformation; treat each as a separate case in the ledger.
- Classify every component in every example as transformed or preserved. Preserved near-matches are crucial negative controls for discovering a selector.
- For any transformed object, record the exact changed coordinates and colors, along with unchanged interior holes and border cells. Infer whether additions depend on shape, size, orientation, completeness, or another condition before applying to the test.
- A visually plausible contour completion is insufficient. Test candidate predicates against all changed and unchanged components, then construct and validate the full output exactly.
- If all demos are exhausted and one submission fails, materially revisit both the object selector and the per-cell transformation. Do not make cosmetic edits to a speculative grid.

This case remains unresolved; it documents process, not a transformation key.

name: continual-arc-four-layer-overlay
description: Use when a 12-row grid has four 3-row panels overlaid cellwise.
---

# Continual-ARC four-panel overlay with precedence

Use when a 12×W input consists of four stacked H×W layers (commonly H=3) that map to one H×W output.

## Procedure
1. Split the input into equal-height panels, in vertical order. For 12×W→3×W, rows 1–3, 4–6, 7–9, and 10–12 form the four candidate layers.
2. Compare each output cell against the four input cells at the matching within-panel coordinate across every demo. Treat 0 as transparent unless evidence shows otherwise.
3. Infer a global priority/precedence order among the nonzero colors from overlapping cells. One observed task used 5 > 4 > 8 > 2 > 0 (highest priority wins). This order is an example only; infer anew for each task.
4. Validate the inferred order on every output coordinate in every demo, especially overlaps among three or more colors and cases where a lower-priority layer is visible because higher-priority layers are zero.
5. Apply the cellwise winner to the test input, retaining the panel-sized output dimensions. Check all row lengths and ensure each output cell comes from a corresponding input coordinate.

## Pitfalls
- Do not simply choose the first or last nonzero panel: precedence may be color-specific, not layer-order-specific.
- An absent color in one example does not establish its priority. Seek overlaps that discriminate candidate orders.
- Do not transfer the example priority 5 > 4 > 8 > 2 to a new task without demos.

name: continual-arc-guide-line-expansion
description: Use when a solid color-2 guide line coexists with a nearby shape and color 8 appears as a full perpendicular stripe.

# Guide-line / perpendicular stripe transformation

A demonstrated Continual-ARC family uses a full-length straight color-2 line as a guide and adds a full-length perpendicular line of color 8, while preserving the original grid contents otherwise. Across six demos, the guide was horizontal or vertical, the background and object colors varied, and the nearby object could be a small irregular shape or a large filled region. In the solved test, the guide was a vertical 2 line at column 14, a small pattern of 0s lay immediately to its left, and the output added a full-height 8 stripe at column 11; all original cells remained unchanged.

## Evidence and cautions

- In all six examples of the demonstrated instance, the new 8 stripe was perpendicular to the full 2 guide line and extended across the full grid dimension.
- Original shape pixels, guide-line pixels, and all unrelated background pixels were retained; the stripe was added rather than replacing the object.
- Stripe position varied with the nearby pattern and its relation to the guide (examples placed it at columns/rows on either side of or within the pattern's span). Therefore, do **not** assume a universal fixed offset from the guide or simply stripe the nearest adjacent column/row. Infer the exact stripe coordinate from the demo object/guide geometry for the current task.
- Some examples also showed apparent displacement or reordering in a broad object region, so compare every input/output cell before deciding whether only the stripe is added. Preserve all content unless the demos establish another operation.

## Workflow

1. Locate a full solid 2 line and determine its orientation.
2. Map nearby non-background shapes and compare all demo differences cellwise.
3. Infer the stripe coordinate and whether any other transformation accompanies it; use examples with changed object geometry to distinguish candidate rules.
4. Add color 8 along the inferred perpendicular full-grid stripe, preserving unaffected cells.
5. Validate dimensions and ensure the stripe is perpendicular and full-length.

# Continual-ARC horizontal gap insertion

Use when task demos show sparse same-color markers along rows and output inserts another color into horizontal gaps.

## Verified pattern
A demonstrated transformation preserves markers and fills background cells strictly between consecutive marker positions in the same row. In the reference demonstration, markers were color 4 on background 9 and every intervening gap cell became 2. The same pattern applied to a test with markers 0 on background 3, using insertion color 2. Rows without at least two markers remain unchanged; cells outside spans remain unchanged. ## Procedure
1. Identify marker, background, and insertion colors from the current task's demos; do not carry colors over from another task.
2. For each row, find marker positions. For each consecutive pair, fill only background cells strictly between them with the demonstrated insertion color.
3. Preserve markers, cells outside spans, and rows with fewer than two markers.
4. Do not extend this rule vertically or beyond marker-bounded spans unless current-task demos establish that behavior.
5. Verify dimensions and ensure no unintended edits before submitting.

## Additional confirmed configuration
A further task used marker 3 on background 6 with insertion color 2. Across irregular, staggered rows, every background cell between each pair of consecutive horizontal markers changed to 2, while all other cells remained unchanged. This confirms that row eligibility is independent: apply the row rule to every row containing at least two markers, even when adjacent rows have different patterns or a marker appears vertically aligned elsewhere.

## Additional confirmed configuration
A current task used marker 6 on background 7 with insertion color 2. Across rows with varying marker counts and staggered positions, every background cell strictly between consecutive markers in each row changed to 2; markers and all outside cells were preserved. This further confirms row-wise, consecutive-marker gap filling with task-specific colors.

## Task-specific instance record: task-8c8e1d50
The task used background 5, marker 0, and inserted color 2. Its 9×21 demo had background 3, marker 8, and inserted color 2; in both, fill only row-wise background cells strictly between consecutive same-row markers. This correctly solved the 12×10 test with zero wrong submissions. This further confirms palette independence and confirms no vertical fill despite aligned markers. The test rows with qualifying marker sets filled their bounded horizontal intervals; isolated/no-marker rows stayed unchanged.

## Important counterexample / resolved selective-gap family
A recurring task family (including task-71ededcc) is NOT simple blanket gap-fill on every axis. Infer from demos which orientation/lines qualify. In demonstrated examples, background 1 or 0, marker color 3/9 or 0, inserted color 2. Rule: for each row and column independently, if its marker cells include at least one adjacent pair (a contiguous run of >=2 markers), fill background cells lying between the outermost markers on that same line with 2; preserve markers and outside cells. Do not fill an otherwise marker-bounded line if its markers are all isolated (no adjacent marker pair). This distinction explains why earlier broad interpolation guesses were wrong.

For task-71ededcc's demos, only rows with adjacent marker runs and columns with adjacent marker runs were completed: demo 1's qualifying rows/columns extend inserted 2s across their marker extrema, while isolated-marker-only lines remain unchanged. The accepted 12×22 test output filled the top and bottom marker-run rows horizontally across their outermost markers, plus vertical marker-run column(s) between their extrema; isolated-only row/columns were untouched. At demo 3, color-3 horizontal top and bottom rows have contiguous marker pairs, and the interior vertical boundary columns have contiguous runs; inserted 2 fills intervening gaps. This is a task-family rule, not a universal coordinate template.

The ordinary horizontal-gap rule remains applicable when demos show all rows with >=2 markers qualify. For selective 2D completion, validate against every demo cellwise and distinguish an adjacent marker pair from merely multiple isolated markers on a line.

## Task-71ededcc recurrence — unresolved, do not reuse failed predictions
A recurrence with test grid 12×18 (background 8, markers 4) was presented with seven demonstrations and eight attempts. All eight submissions failed. It is not a solved rule; use this only as a strong warning and evidence record. Do not repeat the failed outputs or assume the rule is ordinary gap filling, all-axis interpolation, contiguous-pair line filling, or simple transfer from the first demos.

Demos across palettes show marker color varying by example and inserted color 2. Patterns can trigger selective recoloring on rows and columns, and even a complex solid rectangular border (demo 4) produced changes at selected single cells but not a blanket fill. Demo 7's near-solid 4 rectangle with two vertical 0 bars had just one 0→2 change at row 14, column 12. Thus a local shape/object-context selector exists, and rules guessed from aligned marker gaps alone are insufficient.

Eight failed submissions explored broad horizontal fills and combinations of vertical fills in c6/c12/c13, but none was accepted. In particular, all variants based on filling the row5 gap and row10 gap (with or without vertical additions) were rejected. Treat any asserted exact target output as unknown. Future recurrence: request informative demos early, map all changed cells and invariants, infer the selector that identifies target cells, and avoid near-duplicate submissions.
## Evidence scope
This rule has been demonstrated across several color configurations: marker 4 on background 9 filled with 2; marker 6 on background 3 filled with 2; marker 0 on background 3 filled with 2; and marker 8 on background 9 filled with 2. In the latter task, a 13×21 demo and a 27×15 test showed scattered marker-8 positions; fill each same-row gap between consecutive markers with 2, preserving marker cells and all cells outside the bounded gaps. Rows with only one marker remain unchanged. This instance was accepted with that exact transformation. Treat it as a candidate, not a universal ARC rule; verify applicability from each task's demos. # Continual-ARC largest-patch color code

## Trigger
A large grid has a noisy/background field with several spatially localized, dense monochromatic regions, while the output is a small fixed grid uniformly filled with one of the patch colors.

# Continual-ARC marker-selected columns

Use when a bottom row contains isolated 5s and a demonstration suggests those cells select columns for vertical propagation.

## Observed rule
- Each bottom-row 5 marks a column to transform.
- In each selected column, preserve every original nonzero cell. Fill zero cells using the color of the nearest original nonzero cell at or below that row.
- Sweep bottom-to-top: retain encountered source colors and paint intervening zeros with the latest source color. Do not overwrite source cells.
- If no source exists below a cell, leave it unchanged (typically background 0).
- Leave unmarked columns and all other cells unchanged.

A 17×17 demo had three bottom-row 5 markers; selected columns filled upward in color bands, with each encountered original nonzero cell becoming the source color for zeros farther above. A test submission applying this rule was accepted.

Check original nonzero source cells are preserved, cells above the highest source remain unchanged, unselected columns are identical, and dimensions/row widths match.

# Recovery after Continual-ARC rejection

Use this class-level recovery procedure when a test submission receives binary incorrect feedback or a task ID returns in a later stream instance.

1. Treat rejection as evidence only that at least one predicted detail is wrong; it does not identify which cell or assumption failed.
2. Do not resubmit a duplicate or cosmetic variant. Revisit the complete demo evidence and enumerate competing rule dimensions: activation/eligibility, orientation, interval endpoints, color mapping, scope, and preservation of unchanged cells.
3. If task-specific reference notes exist in the skill library, use them to avoid known rejected hypotheses, not as a source of a presumed correct answer. Old notes may be incomplete or based on only some demos.
4. Compare the current demos cell-by-cell, distinguishing established transformations from ambiguous cases. Test each candidate against every demo, including examples where a structure remains unchanged.
5. When candidates remain, request a demo likely to separate them rather than spending an attempt on an unsupported guess. State internally which predictions would differ before choosing the next action.
6. Submit only after a materially revised hypothesis is supported, and validate dimensions, row lengths, colors, and every changed cell.

## Pitfalls
- Broad geometric rules often fit an early demo but fail on later examples with selective eligibility or exceptions.
- A task-specific note marked unresolved is a warning against repeating prior submissions, not an answer key.
- Keep the active Continual-ARC interface strict: one permitted action JSON per puzzle turn, without unrelated tools or prose.

# Guide-line transformation rule transfer caution

A separate task instance showed a full-height color-2 guide at the far-right edge and a nearby color-7 shape on a 0 background. The output added a full-height color-8 stripe at the shape's left edge, parallel to the guide, while shifting the color-7 pattern one column right and preserving the guide. This differs from the known family where a perpendicular color-8 stripe is added without moving the pattern.

Lesson: guide orientation/color and a nearby shape do not uniquely determine the transform. For each task, compare demos cell-by-cell and record (1) stripe orientation, (2) stripe location, (3) whether the pattern is translated or otherwise changed, and (4) what remains fixed. Don't apply a previously seen perpendicular-stripe rule to a superficially similar setup without evidence. See also `arc-reasoning`'s guide-line pitfall; do not assume all guide-line tasks share one rule.

# Shape validation before Continual-ARC submission

A submitted grid can be rejected as invalid before the transformation is even evaluated if its dimensions do not match the required output. This session's test input was 19×16; the drafted outputs accidentally contained 18 rows, so both submissions were structurally invalid regardless of their rule predictions.

Before submitting a same-size transformation:
1. Count output rows and ensure the count equals input height.
2. Count cells in every output row; each must equal input width.
3. Verify each value is an integer in 0–9.
4. Recheck preservation and every changed location against the transformation.

Long hand-written nested arrays are prone to omitted rows. Prefer a row-by-row checklist, indexed representation, or generated grid when tools are permitted. In strict puzzle turns where tools are not permitted, manually enumerate and count rows before sending. Structural validity is a separate check from whether the inferred ARC rule is correct.

# Sparse singleton expansion: unresolved review (task-90835804)

## Evidence observed

Two demos each start with a 1×N row containing a single color-2 marker centered in the row, and expand into an N×N output. For N=5, marker at column 2: color 2 occupies the top center, then symmetric outward-spreading rows at columns `[1,3]` and `[0,4]`; colors 1 appear at `(row 3,col 2)` and `(row 4,col 3)`. For N=13, marker at column 6: color 2 spreads symmetrically from the center, one step farther in each direction per row, through the full-width row at row 6. Color 1 then forms a repeating slanted pattern in lower rows; the final rows include a diagonal/periodic-looking sequence rather than a simple continuation of only the two outward rays.

This establishes an expansion from a centered singleton and suggests a downward fan/triangle for color 2, followed by a second color-1 structure. It does **not** establish the exact rule for coloring all lower rows or whether the lower pattern depends on a period, another geometric rule, or a finite motif. The width-17 test has a centered color-2 singleton, but no observed output validates its full lower portion.

## Rejected predictions and lesson

Two test submissions were rejected. They both used the same color-2 fan through the full width at row 8, then a period-4 color-1 pattern, with the color-1 phase changed between submissions. These are known incorrect predictions; do not retry either phase or treat a visually plausible period-4 pattern as confirmed.

After a first failed prediction, a third demo was still available. The better recovery action was to request that demo to learn the rule for the lower rows, not submit a cosmetically altered phase. For sparse-marker expansions, separate the well-supported initial fan from the underdetermined continuation, and use a remaining demo to discriminate lower-row continuation hypotheses before another submission. Binary rejection does not indicate whether the fan boundary, lower pattern, phase, or another feature was wrong.

# Selective 2D gap-completion recurrence: validation caution

The task's demos support a selective rule candidate rather than blanket interpolation. In each orientation independently, lines with an adjacent pair (a contiguous run of ≥2 markers) received color 2 in background positions between marker positions; isolated-only lines were unchanged. The exact interval endpoint rule must be checked carefully: broad fills of all cells between the outermost markers of an eligible line were rejected on a test after several demos. In the test, horizontal row 5 had separate adjacent pairs at columns 6–8 and 10–12 with a gap at column 9; an attempted fill bridged that gap, and row 10 had marker at col 6 separated from pair at cols 12–13; attempted fill bridged the long interval. These exact submissions were rejected, so evidence says at least one such bridge or another selected fill was wrong, not which individual cell.

Do not regard “adjacent pair makes a line eligible” as enough to establish that all intermediate gaps are filled. Candidate distinctions include fill between each contiguous run only, fill gaps between consecutive markers, fill only selected local gaps, or selecting orientation/line based on additional shape context. Compare exact changed cells for every demo (especially demos with multiple runs or separated markers) before applying. With unresolved candidates, spend a demo on an input that has multiple marker runs on a line and isolated marks aligned vertically/horizontally, rather than repeat broad fill guesses.

# Sparse multi-color arrangement: task-7e1b2dab (unresolved)

This instance had a 30×30 test on background 1, with colored structures 2–9. Two demos were requested and both had 22×22/24×24 grids, also background 1. Each included a 4-shape prototype-like arrangement, sparse two-cell diagonal motifs, and compact multi-cell motifs. Outputs preserved the apparent 4-shape and the compact motifs; the sparse diagonal pairs were expanded/rearranged into additional cells near their regions. A submitted prediction that preserved the apparent 4-shape and compact motifs but locally expanded the sparse pairs was rejected. A second submission which copied/extended those local geometries more broadly was rejected too. Hence this particular visual prototype-stamping interpretation is not validated; no correct rule was identified in the conversation.

For future analysis, do not presume the salient 4-shape is a universal template or that each sparse pair independently anchors a copy. First compare all changed cells in both demos, map per-color components, and account for the compact motifs as well as all preserved cells. Build explicit, competing hypotheses for the relationship among sparse patterns, colors, and output geometry. Treat the rejected output only as a rejection of that complete prediction, not as localization of the error. These notes are a cautionary record, not an answer key.
